reason: The provided sources contain multiple cross-verified claims across independent sites detailing Hubble's discovery of missing oxygen in nearby dwarf galaxies.
story: Dwarf galaxies are tiny cosmic islands holding anywhere from a few thousand to hundreds of millions of stars. Because stars synthesize heavy elements through nuclear fusion, theoretical models predicted these small galaxies should retain a predictable amount of oxygen. But when astronomers analyzed 37 nearby dwarf galaxies using NASA's Hubble Space Telescope, they discovered a startling cosmic heist: massive amounts of expected oxygen were missing. Published in The Astrophysical Journal by the GLOW project, funded by NASA and the National Science Foundation, the study showed that dwarf galaxies hold onto only a tiny fraction of the oxygen their stars create. Powerful galactic winds, driven by massive stars and violent supernova explosions, literally blow the oxygen out of host galaxies into intergalactic space. Thanks to Hubble's unique ability to resolve individual stars in these 37 targets, scientists now know that small galaxies are far more efficient at cleansing themselves of heavy elements than anyone ever imagined.
angle: Dwarf galaxies are missing massive amounts of expected oxygen because supernova explosions unleash galactic winds that blow the element straight out into intergalactic space.

claims.claim: Researchers used NASA's Hubble Space Telescope to analyze 37 nearby dwarf galaxies.
Dwarf galaxies contain anywhere from a few thousand to hundreds of millions of stars.
Astronomers discovered that nearby dwarf galaxies are missing massive amounts of expected oxygen.
Theoretical galactic simulations predict that dwarf galaxies should hold significantly more oxygen than observed.
Oxygen is produced inside galaxies by stars.
Galactic winds unleashed by supernova explosions and massive stars eject oxygen out of dwarf galaxies into intergalactic space.
Oxygen is the most abundant chemical element in galaxies after hydrogen and helium.
The investigation into missing oxygen was conducted by the GLOW (Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds) project.
The GLOW project received funding from both NASA and the National Science Foundation.
Kristen Wingfield McQuinn serves as the principal investigator for the GLOW project.
Grace Telford served as a co-investigator on the dwarf galaxy oxygen study.
All 37 dwarf galaxies studied were close enough for Hubble to resolve their individual stars.
The GLOW study combined Hubble optical imaging with data from NASA's retired Spitzer Space Telescope.
The research team incorporated ground-based radio observations from the Very Large Array and the Australia Telescope Compact Array.
The findings on missing oxygen in dwarf galaxies were published in The Astrophysical Journal.
The Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore conducts science operations for the Hubble Space Telescope.
NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland manages Hubble mission operations.
The Hubble Space Telescope is an international cooperative project between NASA and the European Space Agency.
